title: Morocco province health panels, 2019-2024
text:
Description
Notifiable disease cases, public and private health workforce, and target populations for every Moroccan province and prefecture, 2019-2024, extracted from the Ministry of Health annual reports and checked against their printed totals.
Morocco’s Ministry of Health publishes a yearly statistical report, Santé en Chiffres, as a PDF. Its province-level tables are the most detailed public picture of disease surveillance and health workforce in the country, but they are hard to use: tables change from year to year, blank cells stand for zeros, and place names are spelled inconsistently.
This dataset brings four of those tables for the six editions 2019 to 2024 into clean long-format tables, plus one analysis-ready wide table that joins them.

title: Morocco province health panels, 2019-2024
text:
Origin

Produced by Ministère de la Santé et de la Protection Sociale, Kingdom of Morocco
Published in Santé en Chiffres, editions 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024
Tables used Communicable diseases (tables 79-84 depending on edition); public doctors by network (table 37); public nurses and technicians by network (tables 39-40); private doctors (tables 41-42); target populations by province.
How obtained Tables were extracted from the PDF reports with scripted parsers (position-based column matching for tables where blank cells stand for zero), then province names and region spellings were harmonised.
Published on HDR HDR-MA-0001, version 1.0.0

Origin address: https://www.sante.gov.ma (accessed 2026-07-20). Reuse terms: Publicly released reports. No reuse licence is stated in the reports; HDR publishes the extracted figures with attribution and does not re-host the reports.

title: Morocco province health panels, 2019-2024
text:
Known issues
Read these before analysis.

The list of reported diseases changed in 2022. 2019-2021 reports separate notifiable diseases and diseases under surveillance; 2022-2024 use one surveillance list. COVID-19 appears only in 2022-2023, meningitis only from 2023, rheumatic carditis only until 2021.
Leprosy 2019 is very likely an artefact. The national rate drops from 37.9 per 100,000 in 2019 to near zero from 2021 and never recovers. Run a sensitivity analysis without 2019.
Food poisoning outbreaks (TIAC) 2020-2021 are approximate. The source leaves zero cells blank in these years; blanks were read as zeros.
Casablanca has two grains. Disease and population tables give one unit; the workforce table gives 8 prefectures. The merged file sums them to one unit.
Population figures are programme targets, not census counts. They are revised between editions (2024 total 36.8 million, lower than 2023 at 37.6 million).
Annex tables differ slightly from headline figures, typically by about 1%, likely different data cut-off dates. This dataset reproduces the annex tables.

title: About
text:
Much of the world’s health data is public in name only. The most detailed figures, such as cases by province, health workers by district or births by region, are printed in annual reports as PDF tables. Tables change from one edition to the next, zeros are left blank, place names are spelled differently each year, and documentation exists only in the language of the report. Every researcher who needs these numbers types them again, makes different choices, and cannot cite what they used.
Research teams face the mirror problem. They build careful tables from reports, surveys and registries, use them in one paper, and leave them on a laptop. The next team starts again.
General repositories store whatever is deposited and leave quality to the depositor. International databases publish national averages and modelled estimates, not the subnational figures countries actually report. Between the two, the data that matter most for local health research have no home.
HDR is that home. Anyone can deposit a health dataset. We publish it only if its origin is stated and checkable, describe it in a short note, and give it a DOI so it can be cited like a paper.

title: About
text:
Principles

Origin first. Every dataset names the organisation, publication and address it comes from. A number without a known source cannot be checked, so we do not publish it.
Datasets only. One kind of object, described well. No papers, slides or code deposits.
Checked, not just stored. Every dataset reports checks against its origin, including the ones that do not match exactly.
Honest about limits. Each dataset says in plain words what it is good for and what it is not good for, and lists its known issues before the data.
No silent changes. Published files never change. Corrections create a new version; withdrawn data keep a page explaining why.
Open by default. No login, no fee, open licence, open formats, machine-readable metadata. Every kind of health data is welcome: aggregated tables, patient-level records from trials, cohorts and registries, surveys, and more. Data that could identify a person are published as a catalogue entry with access conditions, and the files stay with their producer.
Regional depth, open door. HDR started in Morocco and knows the sources of the Middle East and North Africa best. It accepts datasets from every country that meet the same rules.

title: About
text:
What HDR is not

Not official statistics. HDR datasets reproduce their origin as faithfully as possible. When a value matters for a decision, check it against the origin named on the dataset page.
Not a place to expose personal data. Patient-level data are published openly only once de-identified. Sensitive or agreement-bound data are listed with their access conditions, not posted.
Not a general repository. For code, papers or images, use Zenodo, OSF or your institution’s repository.

We plan to apply for CoreTrustSeal certification after a year of operation.

title: Rules
text: In one line: no origin, no deposit. Every accepted dataset is published as CSV, Excel and a PDF note, under an open licence, with a DOI.

title: Rules
text:
Acceptance rules
A deposit is accepted only if it meets all ten rules. Rules marked checked by the build are tested automatically before a curator reads the deposit.


R1

Origin stated and checkable
Name the organisation that produced the data, the publication, survey, registry or study it comes from, a URL or DOI where it can be checked, the country of origin and how the data were obtained or derived. A dataset without an origin is refused, whatever its quality. Checked by the build.



R2

Health, and datasets only
Tabular data about health, health care, health systems or their determinants. We do not accept papers, slides, code deposits or images.



R3

Right to share
You must have the right to share the data, and the reuse terms of the origin must allow it. State those terms. Figures from public reports may be republished with attribution; the reports themselves are not re-hosted unless their licence allows it. Terms stated: checked by the build.



R4

Open licence
CC BY 4.0 (default), CC0 1.0, or ODbL 1.0 when the origin requires share-alike. We never publish data under a licence more open than its origin allows, and we do not accept non-commercial or no-derivatives licences. Checked by the build.



R5

Complete, open tables
One UTF-8 CSV file per table, with a header row, at least one row, and every file described. We produce the Excel workbook and the PDF note from your files. Checked by the build.



R6

Every column described
Each variable has a name, a type and a description, with units and missing-value codes where relevant. Labels in the language of the origin are welcome next to the English description. Checked by the build.



R7

Protect the people behind the data
HDR accepts all health data, aggregated or individual-level. Individual-level files are published openly only when they are de-identified: no names, addresses, identity numbers or exact dates of birth, and no combination of variables that singles out a person. The depositor confirms that participants consented, or that an ethics committee or the data protection authority allowed sharing. Data that cannot be de-identified, or that are held under an access or data use agreement, get a catalogue entry with a DOI that describes them and explains how to request access; the files stay with their producer. Counts below 10 that come from non-public sources must be suppressed, with complementary suppression so they cannot be recovered from totals. Figures already published by an official body are accepted as published.



R8

Ethics where needed
If the data come from a research study, give the ethics approval reference, or explain why none was needed.



R9

Honest about limits
List the known issues, say what the data are good for and not good for, and report at least one check of the data against the origin (a total, a subtotal, a published figure). If no check is possible, say why.



R10

Named creators
At least one named creator, with an ORCID where possible, and a contact address for questions about the data. The address is never published.

title: Rules
text:
What every accepted dataset receives

A DOI from DataCite for each version, plus a concept DOI that always points to the latest version. See Cite.
Three formats: the CSV tables, an Excel workbook with About and Variables sheets, and a PDF dataset note.
A landing page with the origin trail, variables, known issues, checks against the origin, a preview, loading code for R, Python and Stata, and the citation.
Machine metadata: DataCite JSON, a Frictionless datapackage.json, and schema.org markup so the dataset appears in Google Dataset Search.
SHA-256 checksums for every file.

title: Rules
text:
How we review

Automatic checks. The build tests rules R1, R3 to R6: origin fields, licence, every file and column described, no empty table. A deposit that fails gets the list of failures back at once.
Origin check. A curator opens the origin and confirms that it exists and that the data come from it.
Spot check. The curator compares at least three values, chosen at random, with the origin, and checks the totals you report.
Decision within 15 working days: accepted, revisions requested (with the list of changes), or refused (with the reasons, quoted from these rules).

Two labels can appear on a dataset page:







Label
Meaning




Origin verified
A curator opened the origin and confirmed that the data come from it.


Checked against the origin
Published checks compare figures in the dataset with figures printed in the origin, and every gap is explained.

title: Rules
text:
Reasons for refusal

No origin, or an origin that cannot be found or checked (R1).
Data the depositor has no right to share, or whose origin forbids redistribution (R3).
Open files that can identify a person, or small counts from non-public sources that are not suppressed (R7). Such data can still be listed as a restricted-access entry.
Values that do not match the origin, without explanation.
Not health data, or not a dataset (R2).

title: Rules
text:
After publication

No silent changes. Published files never change. A correction creates a new version with its own DOI and a line in the version table.
Errors. Anyone can report an error with the form on each dataset page. We answer within 10 working days. Confirmed errors are listed on the dataset page with the version that fixes them, and the reporter is credited if they wish.
Withdrawal. A dataset may be withdrawn if a serious error, a rights problem or a privacy problem is found. Its page stays online as a tombstone that says why; the DOI keeps resolving to it.
Takedown requests. A rights holder who objects to a dataset can write to us. We answer within 10 working days and hide the files while the request is reviewed.
Courtesy to producers. When a dataset republishes figures from a public body, we tell that body and link to its publication.

title: Deposit a dataset
text:
Send your deposit
Send dataset.yml and your CSV files, zipped, to contact address to be added, with the subject “HDR deposit: your title”. We confirm receipt within two working days.
A web upload with automatic checks will replace e-mail once the first deposits from outside the team have gone through.

title: Deposit a dataset
text:
What happens next

The automatic checks run first. If something is missing, you get the list at once.
A curator checks the origin and three values chosen at random.
You see the dataset page and the PDF note before the DOI is minted, and you approve them.
After publication, you can deposit a new version at any time. Earlier versions and their DOIs remain.

title: Cite
text:
Each dataset page and each PDF note give a ready-made citation. The pattern is:

Creators (Year). Title (version X.Y.Z) [Data set]. HDR: Health Data for Research. https://doi.org/10.XXXXX/hdr-ma-0001.v1.0.0

Cite the version DOI, so that readers can find the exact files you analysed. A BibTeX entry is at the bottom of every dataset page.

HDR datasets come from an origin: a report, a survey, a registry or a study. Cite it as well. The dataset page and the note give the origin in full.

title: Cite
text:
How DOIs work on HDR

Every version gets its own DOI, minted through DataCite, for example 10.XXXXX/hdr-ma-0001.v1.0.0.
A concept DOI (10.XXXXX/hdr-ma-0001) always resolves to the latest version.
A DOI always resolves, even if a dataset is withdrawn: it then leads to a page explaining why.
Version numbers follow the rule major.minor.patch: a new table or a change of meaning raises the major number, added rows the minor number, corrected values the patch number.

title: Morocco health system resources by province, 2003-2024

Description
Primary care facilities, public hospital beds and hospital activity for every Moroccan province and prefecture from 2003 to 2024, extracted from all 22 editions of the Ministry of Health yearly report Santé en Chiffres, harmonised to current province codes and checked against every national total printed in the reports.
Morocco’s Ministry of Health has published a yearly statistical report, Santé en Chiffres, since the early 2000s. Its province tables are the only public source on where health facilities and hospital beds are and how they are used, but they are scattered over 22 PDF files whose layout, table numbers and place-name spellings change from one edition to the next. Morocco also created new provinces in 2009 and redrew its regions in 2015.
This dataset puts two decades of those tables into three clean long tables with one code system. Each row names its province, its current region, a comparable unit that stays stable over the whole period, the value, the report page it comes from, and a note when anything was done to it.
Use unit_2004 to build series that span the 2009 province splits: it groups a province with the provinces later carved out of it, so sums by unit_2004 are comparable from 2003 to 2024.

Origin

Produced by Ministère de la Santé et de la Protection Sociale, Kingdom of Morocco
Published in Santé en Chiffres, editions 2003 to 2024 (22 editions, one per data year)
Tables used Primary care facilities (ESSP) by province and setting, and support facilities (public health laboratories, TB centres, reproductive health centres), in every edition. Public hospital beds and activity: one table by province in the 2003-2012 editions, the list of hospitals with province totals in the 2013-2024 editions.
How obtained Tables were read from the PDF reports with scripted parsers that use the position of each number on the page. Province and region names, spelled in many ways across editions, were matched to ISO 3166-2:MA codes with a gazetteer. Every edition was checked against the totals the report itself prints (rows, regions, nation). A printed figure was corrected only when the report’s own sums prove the error; otherwise it is kept as printed and flagged in the note column.

text:
Known issues
Read these before analysis.

Facility counts are not yearly before 2019. Editions between 2007 and 2017 repeat the table of the previous edition every other year; each count is kept once, under its own reference date (15 dates from 2003 to 2024).
Provinces created in 2009 appear from 2009 or 2011. Before that, their facilities and beds are counted in the parent province. Use unit_2004 for series over the whole period.
Provinces without a hospital have no hospital rows (for example Médiouna and Al Haouz in 2003-2004). Absence means none listed, not missing data: province sums equal the national totals in every year.
Hospital values in 2013-2024 come from hospital lists. When the list and the printed province total disagree, the value that makes the printed region total add up is kept, and the note says so (9 province-years).
A few printed values look implausible but are consistent with the report’s totals, for example Taroudant 2015 (679 beds, against about 300 in 2014 and 2016). They are kept as printed and flagged as ‘isolated spike’ in the note (19 province-years).
Patient days or admissions printed as 0 for a hospital with open beds are set to missing (4 values).
University hospitals (CHU) are included in the hospital figures of their host prefecture (for example Casablanca-Anfa, Rabat, Fès, Marrakech, Oujda, Tanger), which explains jumps when a CHU opens (Oujda 2015, Tanger 2023).
